subtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF UNIFICATION PROGRAM

subtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF UNIFICATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Will the minister consider putting a motion on the order paper to reassemble the defence committee of this house with instructions to examine the state of affairs within the national defence department, and with permission to call witnesses including various senior officers who are bringing public attention to the fact that the minister's program of unification will be damaging to Canada's defence forces? I refer particularly to the public interest shown by Generals Simonds and Vokes and Admirals Brock and Landymore, is well as others who are finding fault with this program. I think the public interest requires that something be done in this regard.

It is very gratifying now to see a greater interest being taken in these matters than was the case at the time the committee met earlier this year. So it is my hope that when the legislation is presented to amend the National Defence Act, which I hope will be soon during the course of the current session, and is referred to the committee, there will be real public interest in the discussion that takes place at that time and a searching examination of all the various points of view.

speechtext:
I wish to direct my question to the minister of national resources. In the light of the fixing of May 23 as the date for the opening of the international conference on water for peace at Washington, is the minister now prepared to formulate and state the Canadian government's position on water policy; and in particular
September 6, 1966

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: UNITED STATES CONFERENCE ON WATER FOR PEACE
speechtext:
I apologize, Mr. Speaker, for not responding immediately to the hon. member's question, but I am not used yet to being addressed as the minister of national resources. My title has not been changed officially and I am still referred to as the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys.
I will answer the hon. member's question by saying that we have been informed that the United States government plans to issue invitations to all governments with which it maintains diplomatic relations and to international organizations concerned with water questions. The government, however, has not as yet had the time and opportunity to explore fully the implications of this important initiative on the part of the United States. Considerable concern is felt, however, that such a conference, if it is to succeed, should engage the efforts of other countries not only in its execution but also in its planning. Indeed, the period of time envisaged by the United States for this important preparatory work is not very long if the conference is to be held in May of 1967.
The Canadian government will of course give careful and sympathetic consideration to the United States invitation when it is received. However, the invitation not having been received as yet it would not be proper for me to comment further on the announcement.
In answer to the second part of the hon. member's question let me say we are doing everything possible to develop a Canadian water policy. In Winnipeg recently my hon. friend and I had a very interesting public discussion on that subject. The press was pleased to report that we were very much in agreement on this matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, September 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pickersgill for the second reading of Bill No. C-231, do define and implement a national

September 6, 1966
Transportation
transportation policy for Canada, to amend the Railway Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential provisions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate with some hesitation because of my limited knowledge of the complex field of railway rates and transportation policy generally.
Bill No. C-231 was presented to the house by the minister last Thursday in the course of a very light and witty speech, a speech which caused me and, I believe, many members of this house concern because we had agreed to forgo the resolution stage of the bill in order to co-operate with the government in bringing the legislation forward. Clause 1 sets out the transportation policy and the remaining clauses, which are many in number, attempt to spell out how the government intends to enunciate and carry out that policy. In some respects the bill takes the wraps off the railroads and allows them to charge whatever is feasible, whatever is economically sound or, in some cases, whatever they can get away with.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Over a number of years we have had various transportation boards. This bill sets up one huge 17-man board encompassing all others. This immediately causes me some concern because how can 17 men reach a decision any quicker than the five members of the present Board of Transport Commissioners?
In considering a transportation policy for Canada we must do so with caution because today Canada is at the crossroads in many aspects. In recent years we have seen many policies which have done good but which have divided Canada. In looking back over the transportation history of this country we must realize that it was our transportation and railroad policies which brought Canada together in the very beginning. Those policies must remain sound and must remain fair and just to all parts of Canada or they will have a diversifying effect. You, Mr. Speaker, as well as other members of the house, know that there are too many diversifying elements in Canada today. As members of this house we must ensure that this bill will do nothing to diversify Canada further but will aid in uniting the country as the railway transportation policy did in the very beginning of Canada's history.

In first looking at the bill it seems to me that it is a monstrosity. I see nothing good in it for my part of Canada. This may alarm some members. This bill has been talked about a great deal as being a vast improvement over Bill C-120 which was brought before this house in 1964. How is it an improvement. The Minister of Transport says he would like to see this bill proceeded with with all haste so that the railways might be able to compensate themselves for the minimum wage increase which this house has just assured to the workers. This again causes me some concern because I immediately ask myself, where and how do the railways hope to compensate themselves for this wage increase?
Last week we were told that the wage increase would mean something like $7 million or $8 million for every 1 per cent of increase. We know now what this will mean. With a minimum wage increase of 18 per cent the railways will have to obtain approximately $144 million to $150 million in increased revenue. Where is this going to come from? We are told that the bill will give the railroads the privilege to collect this increased amount of money, and we are told we must proceed with the bill with all haste so that the railways can then start collecting. I think that we as members of parliament owe it to the people we represent to take a very close look at the bill.
First, what does it do? It sets up a 17-man board which, to say the least, will be unwieldly at times. Then it goes on to state what the board will be engaged in. It will be engaged in inquiries; in fact, there will be a continuous inquiry into the whole transportation policy. As the minister said in his opening remarks, the inquiry need not be made public but may be kept confidential. This is stated in the explanatory note on page 26 of the bill. So we have a board to be composed of 17 men which will inquire into all aspects of transportation in Canada and will make rulings as a result of such inquiry. In the past we have had adjustments in the transportation policy which have been arrived at as a result of independent inquiries at which the public could appear. Here we have a transportation board which may in the future carry on inquiries which will be confidential, the results of which may not be made public and which may in some cases be carried out by the very people who perhaps will be trying to substantiate results they have already arrived at. This gives me some concern.
September 6. 1966

It is not necessary that the inquiries of the board which is involved here be made public, nor is it necessary that the recommendations as a result of such inquiries be made public. Certainly I can see that the recommendations resulting from an inquiry will be made public whenever the Governor in Council agrees to carry out those recommendations, but if the Governor in Council should disagree with them I can readily see that those recommendations would not be made public. The bill states that they need not be made public.
In looking at other clauses in the bill we see that various shippers may appear before the board but then the right of appeal is right back to the same board. I see it is suggested that if the chairman is involved in the initial ruling the vice chairman shall preside over the appeal. This is a situation which does not appeal to me as a shipper who might be appearing before the board in argument.
Let us take a look at how the railways will obtain the $150 million increase in revenue which we are told this bill is going to give them the right to collect. First of all we are told that the railroads have not been able to meet their costs because rates have been frozen. We have been told that all freight rates have been frozen since 1959. Actually, only all class rates and non-competitive rates have been frozen since 1959. The railroads have been able to increase their agreed charges and their competitive rates. No ruling by this House of Commons has changed this.
What do these rates account for? What percentage of railroad revenue has been derived from the various rates? Class rates account for 4.7 per cent of their revenue. These figures are taken from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics way-bill analysis for 1964. Non-competitive rates accounted for 29.6 per cent of railway revenue. Therefore while rates were frozen on something like 33 or 34 per cent of railway revenue this bill will take the off wraps in a sense and allow the railways to increase them. In other words, it might well be said that the railways are going to increase these two classes of rates by such an amount that they will be able to collect the additional $144 million to $150 million.
For those who are concerned, I might also add that the statutory rates, which are the Crowsnest pass' rates, account for 13 per cent of railway revenue, competitive rates account for 27.3 per cent and agreed charge rates account for 25.2 per cent. Mind you, there has
Transportation
been no freeze on competitive and agreed charge rates. They have agreed to increase these and have increased them right along. Therefore, according to the 1964 way-bill analysis the railways have increased something like 52 per cent of their revenue in any case.
The other night the minister assured me that as long as he was Minister of Transport and as long as the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was Prime Minister of this country the statutory grain rates, the Crowsnest pass rates, will not be increased and will remain the same.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Let me return to my original analysis of this situation. The increased revenue which the railways must have and which hopefully will result from the passage of this bill will be derived from the movement of goods under the class and non-competitive rates. These account for 33 per cent of their present revenue. Now we come to the crux of the problem.
Where are most commodities shipped under class and non-competitive rates? I want every member of this house to take note of this situation, particularly those members from western Canada and the maritimes because those are the areas from which this increased revenue will be derived. What did Canada's transportation policy mean to the unification of Canada? The transportation policy was the Magna Carta of the west and a basic reason for confederation in the maritimes. This policy had a great deal to do with the uniting of Canada. What does this present bill do? It puts aside those historic facts and, to use a common expression, throws the maritimes and the western part of Canada to the wolves. It does not continue to help unite Canada but rather divides Canada in no uncertain terms. It will have the same effect in some parts of northern Quebec and Ontario.
Let us consider the evidence given before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines in 1964 and 1965 in order to find out the extent of the movement of goods under class and non-competitive rates in various parts of Canada. The table I refer to is printed in a report of the committee for March of 1965 and is dated 1963. It was the most recent table available at that time.
Referring to page 968 of that report we find that goods from western Canada to the maritimes which moved under class and non-competitive rates accounted for 60.7 per cent of

September 6, 1966
Transportation
freight between those areas. Sixty per cent of the movement of goods from western Canada to the maritimes was moved under class and non-competitive rates. This table indicates that 70 per cent of all goods moved from the maritime region to western Canada was moved under class and non-competitive rates. That figure appears at page 973 of this report.
Of all goods moved from western Canada to eastern Canada nearly 50 per cent, actually 44.4 per cent, was moved under class and non-competitive rates. Nearly half of all freight movement from western Canada to eastern Canada moved under these rates. These rates apply to all goods except grain, for example, and the wraps are to be removed to allow the railway companies to increase their revenue by x millions of dollars.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I do not wish to lose my train of thought.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I hope to get the hon. gentleman's train back on the rails by asking this question. The hon. gentleman suggested that the wraps were to be removed from non-competitive and class rates. Does he not realize that the non-competitive rates are to remain under control and, if I understand what he means by "wraps", these rates are to be kept under wrap and will continue to be under control?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I will deal with that point in a minute or two. It is interesting to
note the minister's thinking in this regard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I asked a question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I will deal with that question before I complete my remarks. If I
do not perhaps the minister will ask the question again.
Let us consider the movement of goods from the eastern region to western Canada. This table in the same report indicates that 40 per cent of all goods from eastern Canada to western Canada, including the farm machinery we buy and the automobiles purchased by every Tom, Dick and Harry in western Canada, is shipped under class and non-competitive rates. There is a heavy movement of freight from western Canada to the maritimes and the rest of Canada under non-competitive and class rates.

Let us consider the movement of freight
within the maritime provinces. This same report at page 971 indicates that 55.8 per cent of the movement of all freight within the maritime provinces moved under class and non-competitive rates. That should be of particular interest to the members from the maritimes. The minimum increase in revenue of $150 million will result from the movement of freight now being moved under those rates.
Let us consider the movement of freight in the western region, in which area I have always felt there was a good network of highways. Of all freight movement in western Canada, excluding grain 22 per cent comes under class or non-competitive rates. In western Canada 39 per cent of all freight is moved under the statutory Crowsnest rate and agreed charges rates. Competitive rates apply to 38.4 per cent of all freight movement. The rates in respect of 22 per cent of all freight will be allowed to increase, those in respect of 39 per cent of all movement will remain frozen and the 38.4 per cent of freight movement under the competitive rates will remain relatively the same.
Let us deal with the non-competitive aspect mentioned by the minister when he said that non-competitive rates would remain the same.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I said they would remain under control.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I am glad the minister has corrected me. Let us see under what control these rates will remain. Non-competitive rates will apply to shippers or areas designated as captive shippers or areas. What formula will be used and where will captive areas and shippers be found? I suggest they will be found in the prairies and the maritimes, and the formula that will be used is related to 150 per cent of variable costs. What is the situation regarding areas where competition is keen? This bill states, as was stated in the previous bill, that these rates must be compensatory in relation to variable costs only. In other words, the non-competitive rate will be 50 per cent higher than the competitive rate. We in the west and the people in the maritimes-I was going to suggest the minister also but he is very rarely in the maritimes-will have to pay 50 per cent higher freight rates than people in other areas of Canada.
At page 37 this bill sets out that in not later than three years the commission shall
September 6, 1966

make a study of the Crowsnest pass rates. What will the commission attempt to determine and why is the government suggesting that a study should be made? Surely the answer to that question is that the government hopes a deficiency area can be found in order that the railways can be compensated for their losses and thereby gain increased revenue.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I look at this particular clause of the bill and consider how it will affect me or any other member of the house in running an industry when we realize that within the next three years the government is going to have the commission make a study of that industry and ascertain how large a subsidy, if any, is to be paid after the three-year period has expired. I know what I would do. I would try to minimize my efficiency in the next three years. I would try to paint a picture of dire need of a subsidy as huge as I could logically expect to be paid. This clause is suggesting to the railways that they should be inefficient for the next three years and they will be compensated forever from that time onward.
This clause should be taken out of the bill completely. It is not necessary that it be there. If the government wants to have the commission to be set up make such a study, it can have it do so, but this is what I should like to know from the minister. Does the government feel that the Crowsnest pass rates, with the volume of grain that is being moved today, was moved last year and will be moved next year and in the future, are causing the railways to lose money? If this is what the government feels, let it say so. If it believes that railways will be losing money in the next three years, then it does not have too much confidence in the world wheat situation. I should like an answer to this question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman asked me a question. Would he permit me to answer it right away?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
My answer is that Mr. MacPherson and his commission agreed with the railways that they were losing money on these rates. After full examination we are not convinced of that claim. That is why we took out of the old bill the fixed amount that was to have been paid in respect of these losses and put in instead a provision that there should be an investigation to see whether
Transportation
there were any losses. We decided not to assume, as was assumed in the bill drawn up by the hon. gentleman's friends, which we inherited, and in the bill we introduced-I am not blaming the hon. gentleman's friends because they followed the commission and so did we-that there was a loss. We have now decided not to make any such assumption and to have an independent inquiry to see what the truth is. That is the difference.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Once again the minister is getting a little ahead of me. I was going to deal later with this particular aspect of the report of the MacPherson commission, but I will deal with it right now. Before doing so I want to conclude my remarks with regard to the study of the crowsnest pass rates. I believe this clause is not necessary unless the government feels that today the Crowsnest pass rates are losing money or that within three years they will be losing money and will not provide a proper return for the railways. We must remember that the MacPherson commission report was based upon export shipments of 1958. This is one of the difficulties into which governments get from time to time. They set up commissions to study various questions but before they get around to acting on their reports they are out of date. This is true particularly of the report of the MacPherson commission with regard to the Crowsnest pass rates. I believe that in 1958 an independent study arrived at a figure of a loss of $2 million under the Crowsnest pass rates. This figure was arrived at in connection with moving something like 316 million bushels of wheat for export and a total volume of wheat, including that moved within Canada, of some 450 million bushels.
What did the railways move last year and what do they propose to move this year? The figure is well up in the region of 700 million bushels or 800 million bushels and may be 900 million bushels including coarse grain within Canada. We have nearly two and a half times the volume moved in 1958. How is this volume being moved? It is being moved on the same trackage and in some cases on less trackage. The railways are moving it with modernized equipment and greatly speeded up handling facilities in some cases, although in others there is still a dire need of improved handling facilities.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the MacPherson commission report is outdated with respect to the Crowsnest pass rates and the movement of grain, particularly in light of the increased modernization of handling facilities today. In

September 6, 1966
Transportation
fact, transportation and railway movement have undergone such a change since 1958 that we find optimism in the transportation industry rather than the pessimism that existed in that year because of the desire for wholesale rail abandonment. Today there is not the same desire. Many of those railway lines are paying and in fact I am sure the minister will agree that perhaps only a quarter of the proposed line abandonments are really necessary today in light of the movement of grain and other commodities. This only points up the changed outlook in today's railway movement and in transportation policy generally. We have the movement of potash, we have grain volume tripled, we have every commodity one could mention moving by rail and other transportation facilities in increased tonnages in comparison with the 1958 figures.
I am not going to deal with all the aspects of this bill. The whole rationalization question could be dealt with. The whole passenger question should be dealt with and perhaps will be before the passage of the bill. In summarizing what I have tried to put before the house, Mr. Speaker, I would say this. We are told by the government and the minister that the passage of this bill is important and he urges us to pass it quickly so the railways may begin increasing their revenues to offset the minimum increase in labour costs which they will have to face. subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-231 now under study indicates that the government is preparing to define a general transportation policy for Canada. This new piece of legislation will be known as the National Transport Act.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if we consider the principles of the bill, we realize that its primary purposes are the abandonment of uneconomic railway lines; the abolition of subsidies to railway companies and the removal of the ceiling on freight rates so as to enable the railway companies to increase their rates in order to meet higher current expenditures.
As a matter of fact, Bill No. C-230 passed last week authorized additional expenditures of $170 million by 1967 and of $148 million every subsequent year. This means that in 1968, 1969 and in the ensuing years, the national railway companies will have to anticipate additional expenditures amounting to about $148 million per year.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this bill, as others which we have passed in other areas, will eventually bring about an increase in the cost of living. Eliminating subsidies to the railways and giving them power to increase their freight rates will clearly bring about an increase in freight rates of 10, 15 or even 20 per cent. The companies will not be paying such amounts. The consumers will. We will be paying more for our food, clothes, rents, lumber, materials, etc. In other words, everything will go up. Prices will increase again at a time when we are considering how to fight inflation pressures in Canada.
When the government gave subsidies to the Canadian National, we felt this was nonsensical, because private enterprise such as the trucking industry, for instance, was being taxed in order to subsidize a competitor called the Canadian National. It was complete
September 6, 1966

nonsense to tax private enterprise to maintain a state enterprise; it is neither honest, equitable, or decent toward . the trucking industry.
By eliminating subsidies, we are reverting to competition which, to my mind, is more equitable. This will force the railroads as I said to increase their freight rates. The result will be an increase of the cost of living.
Mr. Speaker, it is not by legislation of this nature that we are going to change the economic situation in Canada. We will be going full speed toward inflation if we pass bills of this nature. We legalize inflation by applying such legislation.
Mr. Speaker, we have been discussing for a long time here, in this chamber, all that legislation of the government seeking to give inflation a permanent hold. When we, Social Crediters, we, of the Ralliement creditiste, ask for increased income for labour, for the Canadian population as a whole, surely it is not through increased freight rates, nor through salary increases, which will have a direct impact on prices. Proof is that we are told that the 18 per cent to be granted to railway workers between now and next year will cost $160 million. The answer does not lie in the 18 per cent or 25 per cent increase, because this goes directly into product prices.
There is another way, which we suggest: It is not for the government to determine rates, no, but it is the government's responsibility to show at all times Canadian consumer requirements with regard to buying power for the purchase of products manufactured and existing in Canada. Legislation should be passed which is aimed at balancing the economic system, and not at further unbalance. We do not want an inflationary law.
When we suggest that the government should use the Bank of Canada to balance the Canadian financial system, this is completely different from what we see in Bill No. C-231, which authorizes a price increase while we propose to use new Bank of Canada credits, which do not figure in prices and which are distributed to each and every Canadian citizen. This means an increase in the income of Canadians enabling them to buy commodities made by Canadians. Seeing that prices are not affected by this additional income, it is therefore clearly anti-inflationary and "anti-deflationary" also. There would never be any danger either of deflation, where people would lack purchasing power to buy the production, or of inflation, i.e. a situation where
Transportation
people would have a purchasing power greater than the country's production.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), the government and all the ministers are aware that our national production this year will reach some $55 billion. On the other hand, Canada's total national revenue will barely reach $42 billion.
How can $55 billion worth of national production be bought up by $42 billion? That is the actual problem; it is too often forgotten, and the government and its economists and advisers are not interested therein. Their main concern is to take away some of the purchasing power from those who do not have too much and give some to those who have even less; this is supposed to balance the economy.
The personal revenue of each individual is not a solution. It is not the Canadian millionaires who prevent the less well-to-do from making a living but the economic system. The millionaire does not eat his millions, he eats food for nourishment, wears clothes, and seldom puts on two suits at once; he wears one at a time.
The rich man also is not the one who prevents the poor man from making a living; it is the financial system which prevents each and every one from sharing in the wealth produced by the natural resources and industry in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, a bill is never introduced to balance purchasing power and national production in Canada. The bills that are introduced settle nothing, or will only help to increase the cost of living, so that the less wealthy will continue to suffer. We have seen this in the passing of Bill No. C-230 which complements or lays the foundation for Bill No. C-231. We do not give an 18 per cent salary raise because of the skill of the worker but because the cost of living has increased. The cost of living has gone up for the railway employee earning $2 an hour as well as for the employee earning $4 an hour. But the 18 per cent pay increase will give to the latter 72c over the next twelve months but only 36c to the former. So, once again, there is a difference, that is double between the salaries of the high and the low wage-earners. Again, the one getting the higher salary will be getting the larger share.
Therefore, a bill is being passed for the benefit of the high wage-earner. But, is the

September 6. 1966
Transportation
pound of butter not selling at the same price for the person earning $2 an hour as for the person earning $4? If the pay increase had been set at a fixed sum for everybody across Canada, it would not have doubled the salaries, for the difference in salary between those earning $2 or $1.50 or $1.25 an hour and those earning $4.25 or $3.75 would have remained the same. Employees would have continued to be paid according to their responsibilities. But this pay increase will not be the same for all the citizens, for all the railway employees, and this applies in any field; for instance, in the mining industry.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that this Bill No. C-231 will cause the cost of living across Canada to rise.
Some members have mentioned uneconomic lines, railway lines which the government will be abandoning soon because they are not bringing in good returns.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
In this case, the service question is involved, the requirements of railroad service or services in certain areas of Canada. There are in the eastern region, in Quebec, in Ontario some unprofitable railway lines; there are some out west, among the farmers of northern Saskatchewan, for instance; there are some in Manitoba. All are nevertheless necessary to serve a part of the population. At such times the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) as well as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and the government consider the question of dollars and cents. To maintain a line in operation no account is taken of the service rendered to the farmer who must ship his grain, nor of the services that must be given to the passengers who may not be in sufficient numbers to make a line profitable. But there again the dollars and cents factor is being considered instead of the social angle, the sheer service angle. A service for the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, I feel the government should be rather concerned with the possibility of passing proper legislation which will ensure service and make financially possible what is physically feasible.
We have been saying it over and over again for a long time. I know that deep inside most members understand the logic of this solution. But we are afraid, we fear to air it, we are afraid to deal with the

financial question. Everybody is being attacked; that is alright. Bills to lessen human beings, to reduce individual initiative, to reduce private enterprise, that is alright. But any legislation to bring finance face to face with the facts, to place finance at the service of such initiatives, those are things the government has no right to discuss. We speak of inflation, yes, but we blame it all on the worker, the manufacturer, the small businessman who has a hard time making ends meet under the present system. They are said to be the cause of inflation.
Mr. Speaker, did you hear the hon. Minister of Finance, or the hon. Minister of Transport, or the government, speak of the interest we pay solely on the Canadian national debt? Is this not a cause of inflation? And no one dares speak about it. Nobody mentions the fact, for instance, that a Canadian purchasing a small home, under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, over a period of 25, 30 and even 35 years, will have paid the price of three homes, once his house is paid for, but received only one-at the end of 25 years, 30 years, he will have paid for three homes and, at that time, his home will no longer be of any value. That is inflation. And Bill No. C-231 is a step in that direction, just as all governmental organizations are.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up any more of the time of the house, but I point out to you and to the hon. Minister of Transport the importance and the urgency of having a clean financial policy for Canada, taking into account realities, not obscure things. Let us be realistic and introduce legislation rendering financially possible that which is physically desirable and feasible.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we would have much less of those disastrous strikes in Canada and we would see a political, economic and social revival that would ensure to workers, farmers and everybody, economic security in individual freedom. That is what the Creditistes want for Canadians and that is what the Creditistes are asking for and demanding of the present government of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few general observations on this bill at this time. We are told that the bill aims to promote the development of a transportation policy for Canada. In that connection I should like to quote briefly from
September 6, 1966

the explanatory note accompanying the bill.
It reads in part as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to define a national transportation policy, to spell out the objectives of that policy and provide the necessary statutory provisions for the achievement of these objectives.
After reading the explanatory note we can look forward with great hope to the accomplishments that will be attained as a result of the passage of this legislation. I am quite sure we all realize that the major work in connection with this bill will be done during the study undertaken by the committee appointed to deal with the legislation, when an opportunity will be afforded to hear representations from various groups in this country.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that we are wondering whether the new transportation commission proposal in this bill will be a repetition of 1938. In that connection I want to quote from today's Globe and Mail what I think is a very appropriate article. It is by Robert Rice Globe and Mail reporter, and reads as follows:
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Will the new transport board be a repeat of 1938?
"It shall be the duty of the board to perform the functions vested in the board . . . with the object of co-ordinating and harmonizing the operations of all carriers engaged in transport by railways, ships and aircraft ..."
-A clause in the 1938 act of parliament establishing the Board of Transport Commissioners to replace the Board of Railway Commissioners. "It is the duty of the commission to perform the functions vested in the commission . . . with the object of co-ordinating and harmonizing the operations of all carriers engaged in transport by railways, water, aircraft, extra-provincial motor vehicle transport and commodity pipe lines . . ."

A clause in the 1966 bill to establish the Canadian Transport Commission to replace the Board of Transport Commissioners, the Air Transport Board and the Canadian Maritime Commission.
It almost seems as if history is repeating itself.
Twenty eight years ago, Parliament gave the job of co-ordinating rail, ship and air transport to the Board of Transport Commissioners.
Six years later, in 1944, it spun off aircraft control and turned it over to the newly formed Air Transport Board. Three years after that, it set up the Canadian Maritime Commission to keep an eye on shipping operations.
And now, in 1966, it is being asked to start all over again and bring the three separate agencies together under one roof, with the added responsibility for inteprovincial trucking and commodity pipe lines.
Will this new move fare better than the ill-fated effort of 1938?
The answer rests with Parliament as it plunges into the intricacies of the government bill to create the Canadian Transport Commission and reform the railways.
Transportation
But assuming Parliament approves the bill largely in its present shape, the real answer will lie in the hands of the 17 members of the new commission.
It will be up to it to achieve the co-ordination and harmony that two royal commissions, almost everyone in the transportation industry, and the present Liberal government feel are essential if Canada is to achieve an efficient, low-cost system of moving goods and people.
I think that is an historically correct assessment of the situation and of the responsibilities that will rest on the 17 commissioners who will be appointed under this legislation.
This subject has been of great concern to the Canadian people over a long period of years. I remember, Mr. Speaker, that when I was elected vice president of the British Columbia Liberal Association the Liberal party at a convention adopted two resolutions which were of particular interest to me at that time. One was to provide for the nationalization of the banks in Canada, a resolution which was adopted at that convention by a majority vote. The second resolution was to provide for a rational transportation policy for Canada.
I must say in fairness that in both these instances the late Senator McGeer was a moving spirit, and I am sure that many of us remember his fight to obtain equitable freight rates for all regions in Canada. However, this revolutionary spirit in the Liberal party soon fizzled out and nothing was done about these two very important resolutions. Consequently, some time later I resigned from the acting presidency of the B.C. Liberal Association and joined the C.C.F. party. That was part of my progressive evolution, Mr. Speaker, if I may put it that way, in political affairs.
Then in 1931 we had the Duff commission which dealt with transportation problems. Then we had the Turgeon royal commission on transportation, which was appointed in 1948 and reported on January 9, 1951. Later we had the MacPherson royal commission, appointed in 1959, and its report lay on the minister's desk for years before any action was taken.
From the formation of the C.C.F. party, and since it has become known as the New Democratic Party, it has recognized the need for a national transportaion policy. I have heard this problem discussed at our national and provincial conventions over a long period of years. Very serious consideration was given to the matter by persons with some knowledge of economics, some knowledge of

September 6, 1966
Transportation
accounting and some knowledge of the requirements of the consumers whom the railways are supposed to serve.
To indicate that the government may be paying lip-service to one of our long-standing policies in the introduction of this bill, I will place on the record the program which was adopted by this party many years ago so that we will know where we stand in this respect. This is in brief the program for which we have stood for a long time. I have been a member of this house for 21 years and have heard this program placed before the house on numerous occasions when this party has urged upon the government the need for a national transportation policy. This is our program:
Transportation is the most important public utility in Canada. In our country of vast distances and widely separated communities, economic and efficient transportation for the bulky primary products of the land, mine and forests is also a factor in linking our various economic regions into one great nation. Narrow profit considerations and lack of a comprehensive transportation policy have helped to produce a complicated and inequitable freight rate structure that has created bitter dissensions between different parts of the country.
An over-all transportation policy based on broad considerations of national interest would integrate, as far as possible, rail, road, water and air services, establish non-discriminatory freight rate scales as a part of the whole transportation plan.
The C.C.F. will also provide federal financial aid to the provinces for highways of national and international importance, including a trans-Canada highway system.
I cite that because here is an indication that in the introduction of this bill the government is at least paying lipservice to the policies which we have advocated throughout the years.
In my opinion the government has missed two outstanding opportunities for the development of a national transportation policy in this country. First, they missed an opportunity at the conclusion of the second world war, when the experience gained in the winning of the war and in the administration of the industries of this country could have been easily used to promote a national transportation policy. I think that the second occasion when the government lost the opportunity was at the time of the building of the trans-Canada pipe line, a time when the government actually provided loans for the building of this very profitable enterprise. I think, Mr. Speaker, that on those two occasions the government would have been well advised to advance the policy they are now advancing in this legislation.
[Mr. Herridge.l
I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the minister on his introduction of the bill, in which he obviously demonstrated that he had a wide knowledge of the subject and of the need for a national transportation policy. He spoke for almost two hours without a note and I though he made an excellent speech. As I say, I listened to it with great interest. I think we can say that the minister knows very well all of the aspects of the problem, but we will have to see what happens in the future to ascertain how his knowledge has been applied with respect to this legislation. When listening to the minister's remarks I could not help but think that here we have a minister who rises so quickly to a point of order in the house but takes so many years to rise to recognize the need for a national transportation policy in Canada.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I also listened with great interest to the speech made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) who indicated a wide knowledge of his subject. I thought he made a most interesting contribution to this debate. It was obvious as one listened to him that he was able to speak from a wide experience so far as western farmers and western conditions are concerned.
The leader of the New Democratic Party, a former premier of Saskatchewan, spoke with full knowledge of the question and of the attitude of western people to the abandonment of lines, passenger services in some instances, and the effect of freight rates on producers. I think it is quite safe to say that no member of this house can speak with greater understanding of this problem, and of the effect it will have on the lives of the producers and people generally in Canada, than the leader of this group. I remember quite well that he was one of the pioneers in our movement who first saw the need for a national transportation policy and urged that need at our national and provincial conventions. It is not a question of getting up here, supporting the legislation that has been brought in, saying amen, and so on. I mention these things to indicate that our movement and our leader in this house were pioneers in promoting the need for a national transportation policy and building up support in the country for that policy.
I thought the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) made a very interesting contribution. He delivered one of those very
September 6. 1966

earthy speeches of his which are always closely related to the soil and the needs of those who cultivate the land, and he demonstrated that he understood the attitude of western producers and their determination to make certain that we have a transportation policy that is fair to all sections of the country.
While the debate on second reading of the
bill has been interesting and informative to many of us-this is a very complicated question and I do not underestimate the difficulties at all; we realize that this is a very intricate, complicated and complex problem-I think we all realize that the real work in connection with this bill rests upon the shoulders of the committee to which the bill will be sent. The committee has a heavy task in this connection. It will have to hear representations. I urge that the committee take plenty of time to deal with this legislation and to get the opinions of those who are concerned.
In connection with the bill I want to make a few suggestions. We attended a very interesting briefing just before we came here. Questions were answered by the minister, the Minister without Portfolio, or by the depar-mental officials who were present, and we were very glad to have the opportunity of hearing the answers. I was a bit concerned about the replies given to some questions, especially those having to do with rationalization. I am just wondering what will become of the railways as a result of what is known as rationalization. I wonder whether rationalization will mean that the Canadian Pacific Railway will continue to operate the Kettle Valley railroad at a considerable profit and yet refuse to grant a daily passenger service, because passenger service alone, it is considered, must make a profit. I hope rationalization will not mean that, and I trust it will not mean the abandonment of certain lines where the freight rates are bringing a nice profit to the company and where a passenger service is required but can only be operated at a loss.
That sort of thing will have to be found out when the committee meets. The committee will have to find out what various terms in the bill mean. I am hopeful that when the bill has been dealt with by the committee and returned to the house the recommendations of the committee will be such that I shall enjoy the opportunity to ride on the first passenger train to run again on the Kettle Valley railway.

MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. changed certain accounting methods which had the effect of increasing 1965 net profit by $3 million.

Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the bill before us is lacking in concept. I do not wish to say this in an unduly critical way but, like so many members on this side of the house, I feel the measure should have been referred to a committee at an earlier stage than is now proposed. In these circumstances we have no alternative but to vote against the bill as it now stands on second reading.
I have said that the approach taken to the subject has been incorrect. I take this position because I find that the issue is based in a large degree on past experience, and when I say "past" I mean the comparatively recent past, even four or five years ago. In this connection I shall refer later to speeches which I have made in this house as late as the present year, 1966.
I am surprised that the government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) in particular have not given the whole subject of this legislation much greater consideration because in my view a great deal more consideration is required. During the present debate a number of speakers have pointed out how rapidly the situation is changing. The concept of railroading is changing almost from day to day, particularly in the area of freight rates. As an example of changing patterns I merely draw attention to the fact that the movement of wheat has practically doubled in the past four or five years from 400 million to 800 million bushels. This in itself, it seems to me,
September 6, 1966

is reason enough why all those concerned should be allowed to present their views on the subject to a committee of parliament before this bill progresses further.
In this context I have in mind particularly the representatives of the labour organizations, those who represent the provinces and the municipalities, and those corporations from one end of this country to the other which are directly affected by transport legislation. Let us not forget that this bill does not merely affect certain parts of the nation. It affects western Canada, northwestern Ontario, northern Quebec, the whole country, in fact, with the exception of a relatively small area which may be indicated by drawing a line from Montreal to Windsor. I believe that an opportunity should be given to all concerned, right down to individuals, to express their views to a committee before the bill progresses to a point at which there is no recourse. We have accepted this principle in the case of other bills.
I appeal to the minister to consider seriously whether the course I have suggested cannot be taken. As I say, I do not wish to appear unduly critical. We who sit on this side of the house do not like to be criticizing continually without offering constructive alternatives. I say that the alternative is to send this measure to the committee first, not at some later stage, so that the house in reaching its conclusions may take into consideration the opinions of the people I mentioned earlier.
I enjoyed the reference by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) to the Kettle Valley because it is very close to my own constituency. We hear a great deal about the Crowsnest pass rates. For us, of course, the Crowsnest is part of the Kettle Valley line running from Lethbridge to Nelson and through the Kettle Valley to the coast.
I have suggested that this bill is preoccupied with the conditions of the past. In my opinion it should be based on the present and it should also look forward for a few years at least. It is most disappointing. I would point out again, as I did in a speech I made in this house on February 9, that when farmers move wheat, vegetables or other crops out of their areas they spend the money they receive on other goods produced, more often than not, in Canada.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I might refer specifically to the time nearly 25 years ago when I had a heating unit put in my farmhouse in Alberta. It was ordered
Transportation
from Montreal, and I think I can recall the actual address. I believe it was 242 Jarvis Street. I was reminded of this the other day when an hon. member of this house crossed the floor complaining in a sense about something like this. I thought that the rest of us showed much better sense many years ago than he was showing. As a matter of fact, this was at a time when he was a very young man I am proud of that fact and I simply present it to emphasize part of my argument.
Whenever we make a profit in western Canada the money immediately becomes available to the rest of Canada. We are proud of that. This is part of our argument; this is the reason we so often have seemed to demand a certain service. I pointed out too in the same speech that the railway service is the worst we have had in history. Many excuses were offered and there were even investigations instigated. On February 7, as a matter of fact, the Board of Transport Commissioners authorized a probe into customer service. The emphasis of the inquiry was on a move the C.P.R. had made to improve customer service in respect of box cars.
At that time I tried to point out that the service had not been improved. A probe was instigated and apparently it showed that this was not the case. On Tuesday March 1, I pointed out the same thing again. There was nothing much done about it. The minister who speaks for the Canadian Wheat Board had some statistics which showed that the quotas were higher than actually was the case. These were given to him no doubt by the railroad or by the Wheat Board, but they were not correct. A day later I again pointed out what these charges meant and what the lack of service meant. I hope the minister will consider this matter because in legislation such as this we are looking forward. If we are not looking forward more than we were four or five or 30 or 40 years ago, if we are not looking forward having in m'nd the facts of today, then in my opinion we are not looking forward far enough.
This may sound a little like a chronology, but on March 4 I received a letter from a prominent man in the farm union who had gone to Vancouver in an effort to see what was the matter out there. He looked into the whole problem. As we pointed out at that time, it was not wholly the fault of the railways, but we are reminded of all these things when we are faced with a bill like this.

I am reminded also of passenger service, and if time permits I should like to go into that a little as well. On March 17 the statement was made that it seemed that the C.P.R. was not concerned about our area. It seemed that there were empty box cars going by local points to Calgary and Medicine Hat when the elevator companies had local orders for delivery to Calgary and Medicine Hat mills. I think these things should be brought to the attention of the committee and through the committee to the house.
I should like to go back to March 7 and a headline which reads, "Wheat Moves At Record Clip". This was a release by the C.P.R., as a matter of fact, which appeared in the Lethbridge Herald of March 7. This sounded good to me. As a matter of fact I even went to the telephone and called some people at home. It said, "the wheat growers are happy now." The answer was, "what are you talking about". I looked at the headline again. I began to look into it a little deeper. I looked at the profits of the C.P.R. and began to think that "clip" meant something other than speed. When you clip horses and cows for hair and sheep for wool and you come out with a record yield on clip, you have a record take. When I looked at the take of the C.P.R. generally and particularly in our area I rather enjoyed reading this headline, "Wheat Moves At Record Clip".
I do not make any claim to understand this bill as much as I should but, generally speaking, if the bill goes through with these increases I believe that the people in my area and those of northern Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes will take a very dim view of the people who represent them in this house. I think they would take a very dim view if we stood up, said our piece and then let the bill pass without opposition before we are assured there is full realization on the part of the minister and the government that railway shipping in particular is different from what it was four or five years ago and certainly much different from what it was 30 or 40 years ago.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I pointed out before the situation in respect of wheat. Hon. members have heard this before but I want to emphasize it. There are also the potash shipments, and in farming areas an increase in the volume of shipments has been brought about by mechanization and automation on the farm the application of new farming methods such as the utilization of fertilizer and things like that. As a prime example I might mention my own farm

which I have farmed for 30 years. In my area we have had a most abundant crop. I have seen many good crops. This harvest we have had a particularly good yield. It was 30 bushels more than anything I could possibly imagine as a result of my own experience. The high yield was prevalent throughout the area and related not only to grain but small crops such as peas, beans, corn, cucumbers and many others. This not only will apply to agricultural products in the west but to the production of primary products-iron ore, pulp, etc.-in the eastern areas mentioned before, Quebec and northern Ontario, as well as the hard goods manufactured and shipped from the industrial area.
There has been a tremendous increase in production throughout the country which has given a boost to the Canadian economy. When a government considers a major revision such as the one embodied in the bill now before us, one which will probably be with us for 50 or 60 years, it should keep all the factors I have mentioned in mind. The Canadian public is aware of this increase in our productivity as are the railway companies who are taking advantage of it. One need only consider the railway companies' returns, the increase in the value of their stock and their increased dividends.
Why have the minister and the government not considered fully all the factors involved? Why has this bill not been drafted in a way that would indicate that due consideration has been given to its intent? Surely it is reasonable to ask that we be given an opportunity to hear from witnesses who have something to say about transportation in Canada before this house deals with a measure of this magnitude. I realize that not every member is interested in this type of thing, and that is only human nature. Some of us are interested in the operations of railways, some of us are interested in the price of bread, butter, eggs and fish, while others are interested in the Canadian economy generally. I urge the minister and the members of this house to consider this bill in the proper light. I appreciate the time I have been allowed to speak in this house and I hope the minister will consider some of the matters I have raised.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to make a
September 6, 1966

few comments on Bill No. C-231 which is intituled:
An Act to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada, to amend the Railway Act and other Acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential provisions.
By this bill the federal government seeks to set up a Canadian transport commission and to provide for all modes of transport which come under federal jurisdiction such as railways, trucks engaged in extra-provincial activities, aircraft, coastal and inland vessels and pipe-lines.
Mr. Speaker, there has been a terrific expansion of transportation in the past ten years or so. As far as shipping is concerned, the St. Lawrence seaway has enabled Canada to make great progress in the fields of transport and trade by waterways.
Air transport has been characterized by the same dynamism in the last six years since another carrier, Canadian Pacific Airlines, is now in operation besides Air Canada. Other routes have been inaugurated which make Canada justly proud of the air services it provides for its citizens and foreigners.
In addition, over the past ten years there has been obvious and noticeable progress in transportation, especially in motor vehicle transport. That advance, that progress is due to the Trans-Canada highway which now links Canada from coast-to-coast and which allows for the efficient and speedy transport of passengers and freight by road.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Ten years ago highway transportation between or within the provinces was faced with many problems.
Finally, we note that during that decade, the railways, which were up against a keener competition from increased water air and highway transportation, have nevertheless continued to develop thanks to the many subsidies granted by the federal government, and the yearly subsidies they have received, especially since 1960. This brief review shows that water, air and highway transportation have made inroads upon the monopoly of transport held almost exclusively by the Canadian railways a dozen years ago.
Of course, this bill is very important and it was actually time it was introduced in this house, since a royal commission had made very worthwhile recommendations and suggestions many years ago. I am speaking of the MacPherson commission.
Transportation
Of course, some reforms are called for and co-ordination and standardization regulations should be encouraged with regard to those four means of transportation, not to mention the field of pipeline transportation.
But, Mr. Speaker, if some reforms and standardization are advisable, this does not mean that everything must be changed overnight and that the useful contribution to the country of certain means of transportation, such as trucking, should not be retained. In all fairness to thousands of Canadians and several areas of the country, the characteristics of some areas must also be taken into account. The assistance which must be continued must promote the economic development of those particular areas. When I speak of areas, I think above all of the western provinces and the maritimes. We must continue to give assistance, not token assistance, or on a ridiculously low scale, but substantial assistance, because if we consider here in parliament an economically strong Canada, on the road to progress, not only as a whole, but in all its important parts-and the ten provinces are important economically-the federal government cannot afford, whatever the legislation, to pass drastic and expeditious measures which would put some areas of Canada at a disadvantage.
And when I hear the fears expressed by hon. members from the maritimes and western Canada, I congratulate them for taking a stand and warning the government, and the officials who will see to the administration of the new transport board of Canada, against proceeding too quickly in the administrative field with regard to unification and co-ordination. We will have to try to avoid serious discrimination, so that Canadians from coast to coast will not see in the field of transportation discrimination from one area to another or from one transportation system to another but will feel that throughout the country, whether they live in the west, in central Canada, in the maritimes or elsewhere, the laws of the central government do not discriminate against any Canadian because he lives in one province rather than in another.
Some recommendations of the MacPherson commission apply to uneconomic railway lines. For instance, in the notes which have been sent to us by the officials of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), it is indicated that the commission recommends that the railways should not be asked to

September 6, 1966
Transportation
subsidize their uneconomic services through their economic ones, that the freight services should not subsidize the passenger services. The commission also mentions that the railways must, in the public interest, operate uneconomic services; that is when the commission recommends that the costs be borne by the public treasury. Also, with regard to transportation by rail, the MacPherson commission mentions the Crowsnest pass rates and the rates applicable to export grain. It is understood that those rates must be maintained and that the losses suffered by the railways, if any, must equally be borne by the public treasury.
In the recommendations of the said commission, mention is made of special assistance to the Atlantic provinces, of the principle of special assistance to the Atlantic provinces which should be maintained and of a special study to be made so as to determine whether the principle could not be more efficiently implemented by other means.
Evidently, such Canadian transport commission must meet all the complex problems of Canada and that is why at this stage, I do not intend to say any more on the various viewpoints we could bring up on this bill. We know the legislation will be referred to a parliamentary committee; we trust, Mr. Speaker, that interested individuals will be called before the committee and that it will even be authorized to travel so as to observe the material, economic and equitable conditions of various methods of transportation in the various areas of the country.
To-day, I should like to state two points of view lingering in my mind with some concern. Involved is highway transport which the national commission would take over. My second remark, which I shall revert to in closing, bears on the future attitude of the railways toward highway transport.
Will the railways, like the C.N.R. for instance, be in a position to continue to intervene, by all kinds of direct and indirect means, with highway transport and compete with it in an underhanded way, particularly in relation to trucking?
When speaking of transport, Mr. Speaker, we refer, evidently, from the constitutional standpoint, to the British North America Act, especially to subsection 10 section 92 which stipulates the constitutional authority in the field of transport. Obviously, section 92 does not give in detail the modern means of transport because in 1867, there was no trucking,

no automobile transport, and the various aspects of transport could not be mentioned. That subsection 10 of section 92 reads as follows:
Local Works and Undertakings other than such as are of the following Classes:
Evidently, section 92, subsection 10, gives exclusive authority on local works and undertakings other than those mentioned in (a),
(b), (c).
This means that (a), (b) and (c) come under federal authority. Those exceptions in subsection 10 of section 92 are indicated as follows:
Lines of Steam and other Ships, Railways, Canals, Telegraphs, and other Works and Undertakings connecting the Province with any other or others of the Provinces, or extending beyond the Limits of the Province.
Consequently, when the federal government and the minister introduce a piece of legislation, concerning, for instance, interprovincial, international or extra-provincial highway transport, the minister is in a very good constitutional position, since according to the letter and the spirit of the constitution, authority is conferred on the central government in the field of interprovincial transport. This was confirmed by the Privy Council in London in a decision rendered on February 22, 1954, in the Winner case.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to read the main paragraphs of that Privy Council's decision which enable us to reconsider together the position and the constitutional decisions rendered in the field of interprovincial transport.

The power of a province to control its own roads does not entitle it to interfere with connecting undertakings that fall within section 92(10) (a) of the British North America Act or impair Dominion jurisdiction in relation thereto. Legislation of a province which denies the use of provincial roads to such an undertaking or sterilizes the undertaking itself is an interference with exclusive Dominion authority. Whatever provisions or regulations a province may prescribe with regard to its roads, it must not prevent or restrict interprovincial traffic. It may, of course, prescribe traffic regulations but its legislation must be confined to such matters.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It is not desirable nor is it possible to define precisely the limits within which use of provincial highways may be regulated. Nor need the court be concerned with the question whether a province was entitled to plough up its roads and so make interprovincial connections impossible. So isolationist a policy was unthinkable. The roads existed here and in fact formed a connection with other provinces and with another country. It is immaterial
September 6, 1966

that the Dominion has not legislated in relation to a connecting undertaking. A province is precluded in any event from interfering with it.
Provincial legislation is ultra vires where it prohibits the operator of a particular connecting undertaking, namely an international and interprovincial bus line, from using provincial highways except as a means of passage from another country to another province, as where it purports to prohibit it from bringing passengers into the province or carrying passengers outside the province or between points within the province. Such legislation cannot be justified as traffic regulation.
Where an undertaking is in pith and substance interprovincial, and in its operations embraces, in the same way, both interprovincial and intraprovincial journeys, it is wrong to say that its intraprovincial operations are incidental and hence subject to provincial control. If the undertaking is in fact one and indivisible, then merely because it might have been operated differently by limiting its activities to activities within or without the province, does not make it any less an interconnecting undertaking. Hence, its intraprovincial operations cannot be severed for the purpose of committing them to provincial legislative jurisdiction.
Of course, a carrier who is substantially an internal carrier cannot put himself outside of provincial jurisdiction by starting his activities a few miles over the border. Such a subterfuge will not avail.
Quaere, whether the operator of the connecting bus line in this case could initiate a purely provincial bus service even though it was under the aegis of and managed by his present organization!

Those are very important and relevant provisions which, in my humble opinion, should be put on record for further reference during this debate or even during the discussions to be held or the studies to be made by the parliamentary committee.
As I was saying earlier, under the constitution, the minister and the federal government are empowered to act with regard to interprovincial, extra-provincial or international transport.
But it has happened, and this fact should be taken into account here in Ottawa, that for almost a century all legislation and even regulations in the field of interprovincial transport have been left to the provinces.
Indeed, the legislation recognizing this practice is included in the federal statutes themselves. With regard to these precedents, I should particularly like to point out to this house the federal legislation concerning extra-provincial transportation by motor vehicle, which is included in the Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 59. This legislation was passed on June 26, 1954, therefore following the judgment given in February 1954 in a
Transportation
case heard by the Privy Council which recognized the constitutional authority of the central government. Here, however, in practice the central government of Canada referred the problem of interprovincial transport to the provinces, probably because transportation of that sort was not very important ten years ago on account of the lack of organization in the interprovincial system and because the Trans-Canada highway had not yet been built.
Now, this has always been done and is still being done, and that federal act of June 26, 1954, admitted it in its terms and provisions.
I want to remind the house in particular of subsection 2 of section 3:
The provincial transport board in each province can, at its discretion, deliver to a person a licence to operate an extra-provincial enterprise by entering the province or passing through it under the same conditions and in the same way as if the extra-provincial enterprise operated there was a local enterprise.
And also in section 4 of that same bill:
4. When, in a province, the tariffs and rates to be set by a local carrier for local transport are determined or regulated by the provincial transport board, the tariffs and rates to be set by a federal carrier for extra-provincial transport in that province can, at the discretion of the provincial transport board, be determined and regulated by the provincial transport board in the same way and under the same conditions as if extra-provincial transport in that province were local transport.
Therefore, the texts of that act clearly show that the federal government has until today delegated to the province; the power to legislate and regulate in the field of trucking.
And now, in the present bill setting up that federal transport commission, the federal government wants to recover its authority on interprovincial trucking and its administration as well.
The Department of Transport created in 1964, when considering that matter, a group of officials to study trucking in particular. It would seem that the federal government decided also to intervene in the field of trucking for three main reasons. Since 1954, interprovincial trucking has greatly increased thanks to the construction of the Trans-Canada highway, so that it has become truly competitive with regard to the railways. Trucking is becoming some kind of economic and commercial giant in the field of interprovincial transport, and there is no doubt it can harm the railways which are facing

September 6, 1966
Transportation
some difficulties. The railways and interprovincial trucking come into conflict quite often with regard to the delivery of permits and the initiative which should or should not be left to the railways to add to their services a trucking service to round out their obligations. In fact, it seems that the railways must use trailers or trucking systems to compete with the private trucking industry.
The Department of Transport also seems to think that it is a good thing to have the -trucking industry and the other means of -transport come under the same commission, because the MacPherson commission, which studied all those complicated problems, recommended it and, in the areas where competition between the various systems of transportation is particularly keen, it would be better that only one act, one set of rules apply to all transportation systems in Canada.
Finally, according to this study committee and certain declarations which were made previously by the hon. Minister of Transport, and the hon. Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Turner), who is with the Department of Transport, it appears that this would enable the central government to fulfil its obligations, as he says, to control economic development in Canada from sea to sea.
If the federal government is considering taking over highway transport, I believe this would be doing a certain injustice particularly toward the Canadian Trucking Association and the private truckers, and also toward the Quebec Trucking Association, Incorporated. Because, in hard times, say for the past ten years, while they extended further within the provinces, from one province to the other. By placing interprovincial trucking under its own jurisdiction, the federal government is obviously hurting directly the interprovincial trucking industry. As a matter of fact, representatives of this industry, that is the Canadian Trucking Association and the Quebec Trucking Association, have already made representations to the government and to the minister in this regard.
September 6, 1966



Now, over those ten years, while highways within the province as well as the Trans-Canada highway were being constructed, carriers and road transport companies across the country have developed a trucking industry which is strongly competing with other means of transportation. They have shown a lot of aggressiveness and co-ordination in their efforts, in their activities, and have helped the country and the province of Quebec considerably, as far as the Quebec Trucking Association is concerned.
To-day, of course, those associations fear that by placing the road transport industry under the sole jurisdiction of the federal government the national transportation commission will be used as a means to permit the railways to carry on a competition which is becoming very difficult to meet. While the truckers and those involved in those companies succeed in spite of many difficulties in operating at a profit, they have to withstand the competition of the C.N. which operates with a deficit, of course, and which must deal with unprofitable services and with some branch lines, a situation which will apparently be corrected under the present legislation.
I should like to call the minister's attention to a paragraph of the Canadian Trucking Association brief on this subject. On page 3 of the brief presented, in January 1966, we read the following:
In the field of transportation, unrestricted competition will only bring back monopoly conditions. This should not blind us to the danger of excessive regulations or poor regulations. The standard is simply this: Are the regulations contributing to maintain transport services and continued competition?
At the present time, jurisdiction over trucking operations is split between the federal and provincial governments. Under current federal legislation, extra-provincial regulation policies are implemented by provincial boards completely without any co-ordination or even uniformity whatever between them.
Very little satisfaction is obtained from such a system by extra-provincial trucking contractors.
The present system under which extra-provincial truck transport is ruled by a certain number of individual regulatory boards, each operating under a different code and under provincial regulations is utterly impractical. The fact that they achieve a certain degree of effectiveness is a tribute to the common sense and intelligence of the members of the provincial boards. But to be practical-
And the brief continues with this conclusion:
What we need is uniform and co-ordinated regulations.
